tei:titleStmt.tei:title: גאולה לשבת לפני שבעות
Geulah piyyuṭ for the Shabbat before Shavuot, by Rabbi Yehuda bar Shmuel he-Ḥasid of Regensburg

tei:div.tei:head: Geulah piyyuṭ for the Shabbat before Shavuot, by Rabbi Yehuda bar Shmuel he-Ḥasid of Regensburg

tei:lg.tei:l: You lifted the dove on the wings of eagles,
and nested it in Your lap in the innermost chambers.
Why have You abandoned her, wandering among the forests?
And from all passers-by casting nets,
strangers incited to other gods,
and she, in the hidden places, cries to the Spouse of her youth.
And she raises her pupil to her first Spouse,
and between Etzer and Dishon her tongue slips to Them,
For I know that you have no other Redeemer. to ask: “Why did you leave my soul?
How could the pure one forever go with hair uncovered?
Mizzah and Shammah to shame and disgrace!
And the slavegirl’s son startled me in fear,
for with a high hand he cast the bow.
And the shrine’s tents to Oholivama,
And my tent, how long and how much will you wait?
There is no wonder, there is no sign, and there is no vision or sight,
and were I to ask to see when is the final miracle,
prophecies would answer, “You made it hard to ask...
for I know that you have no other Redeemer.
Ushered into exile were the gentle daughters from the provinces,
and from verdant tribes, and from tranquil resting-places,
and they were scattered among people lacking understanding,
with alien dialects and strange languages.
How could the guardians of faith be buried among them?
who have no desire to answer to iconized godlings?
Why do You stand afar, o Dweller in the Welkin?
My Beloved withdraws, and my subjugator stresses!
For I know that you have no other Redeemer. For the End of Dawes we ask, yea, ask!
Down came the flag of love from over me, and the prideful foot set a yoke upon me.
And I am punished, cruelly removed,
an exile and prisoner, and bitter and angry and sullen.
There is no crown-prince nor marshal, no king and no noble.
The stressor turned towards me, and the Rock turned from me.
They destroyed in Their fury the place Their sole walks.
And They ignited in Their anger Their doorpost and Their lintel.
And fire fevered in Their rage and kindled unto the underworld.
For I know that you have no other Redeemer.
Always will my Master abandon? Is there no conclusion to my wondrous visions?
Arise, Cause, and may my adversaries be scattered,
and return to my abodes, to the temple’s midst,
and bring upon my neighbors requital for our sorrow,
and reveal to my eyes as You came upon Sinai!
and with dew of salvation descend upon the reverent and awed,
and bring down the rebellious slavegirl’s son from my seat,
till I no longer descend in sorrow to the underworld,
for I know that you have no other Redeemer.
For the parents’ sake You will save the children
and bring redemption to their children’s children.
Blessed are You, Cause, who redeemed Israel.

tei:note.tei:p: Two sons of Seir the Horite, mentioned in Genesis 36:21. Here representing Christianity and the diaspora as a whole.
Ruth 4:4. A repeated refrain throughout the poem.
A sign of disgrace, see Numbers 5:18 and the sotah ritual.
Two grandsons of Esau, mentioned in Genesis 36:13 and 17. Here representing Christianity.
Ishmael son of Hagar. Here representing Islam.
A weapon associated with Ishamel. See Genesis 21:20
An untranslateable pun — “the shrine’s tents” is oholei vama
One of Esau’s wives, see Genesis 36:2. Perhaps referring to the Crusader conquest of Jerusalem.
Another untranslateable pun — “my tent, how long” is oholi va-ma
Another untranslateable pun, in this case a spoonerism. “My Beloved withdraws” = dodi raḥaq, while “my subjugator stresses” is rodi daḥaq.
An obsolete Middle English plural of day, to reflect the unique plural form yamin used here, based on the Aramaic-influenced form of Daniel 12:13.
Another untranslatable pun. “Stressor” = tsar, while “Rock” is tsur.
Ishmael. Find note above on “the slavegirl’s son.”
